issues.description: The manuscript alternately describes the study as a national probability/general-population NZAVS study and as an introductory-psychology participant-pool study with 374 mostly young students. These are mutually incompatible sampling frames. This undermines the design description, generalizability claims, and interpretation of all analyses.
issues.quote: “We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years.” / “We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.”

issues.description: If the methods section is correct, the sample is small, young, disproportionately female, and predominantly Pākehā, not representative of the New Zealand population. This makes general-population conclusions and claims about national representativeness invalid.
issues.quote: “Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European).”

issues.description: The manuscript states that participants were recruited from a university participant pool but then refers readers to the NZAVS website for details. The relationship between the participant-pool sample and the NZAVS is unclear, making the data source, recruitment procedure, and sample frame impossible to verify.
issues.quote: “Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.”

issues.description: Longitudinal studies require reporting the original sample size, wave-by-wave retention, attrition patterns, and whether attrition is related to key variables. The manuscript defers retention information to a website and then uses listwise deletion, preventing evaluation of attrition bias.
issues.quote: “Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.”

issues.description: Listwise deletion in a five-wave longitudinal design can substantially reduce power and bias estimates unless data are missing completely at random. The manuscript does not test or justify the MCAR assumption and does not use more appropriate approaches such as FIML or multiple imputation.
issues.quote: “Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.”

issues.description: The timing of the five measurement occasions is ambiguous. The manuscript says five semesters but also describes a five-year span from 2009 to 2013. Cross-lagged estimates depend on the interval between waves; unequal or unclear intervals make the stationarity assumption and interpretation of lagged paths questionable.
issues.quote: “This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).”

issues.description: The manuscript claims to analyze willingness to sacrifice/change behavior, but the methods describe two items assessing concern and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. These are different constructs. Conclusions about willingness to make sacrifices or behavior change are not supported by the stated measure.
issues.quote: “Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, ‘How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?’ and ‘To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?’”

issues.description: The study frames the outcome as willingness to change behavior, but the listed items measure environmental concern/skepticism, not actual behavior or even behavioral intention. This invalidates behavioral interpretations.
issues.quote: “people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment”

issues.description: Much of the introduction, abstract, and discussion frame the study around climate change denial and mitigation, but the reported environmentalism items concern the natural environment generally and whether environmental problems are exaggerated. Climate-change-specific beliefs, denial, risk perception, or mitigation behavior were not measured.
issues.quote: “Research on the psychological foundations of climate change denial have highlighted the important role of two ideological attitudes”

issues.description: The environmental scale contains an item that must be reverse-coded to represent pro-environmentalism. The manuscript does not state whether reverse coding was performed or how the items were combined, impairing replicability and raising concern about score interpretation.
issues.quote: “‘To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?’ Participants responded on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much)”

issues.description: The manuscript lists selected SDO, RWA, and environmental items but does not specify whether items were averaged, summed, modeled as latent indicators, reverse-coded, or otherwise transformed. This is especially important because SDO includes equality-favoring items and environmentalism includes a reverse-keyed item.
issues.quote: “Three items favoured dominance, such as ‘To get ahead in life, it is sometimes okay to step on other groups’, and three favoured equality, such as ‘We should have increased social equality’.”

issues.subcategory: missing RWA item at one wave
issues.description: One RWA item was not administered at Time 2, meaning the RWA measure is not identical across waves. Without explaining how this was handled or testing measurement equivalence, longitudinal changes may reflect measurement differences rather than true change.
issues.quote: “The item ‘Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done’, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.”

issues.description: Longitudinal comparisons and cross-lagged paths require evidence that constructs are measured equivalently over time. The manuscript reports constraints on residual variances but does not report tests of configural, metric, scalar, or residual invariance, despite using shortened scales and one missing RWA item.
issues.quote: “We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.”

issues.description: The study uses six-item short forms for SDO and RWA and reports that reliability is poorer than full scales. Low reliability attenuates and can distort cross-lagged effects, especially when comparing predictors. Reliabilities are only discussed at Time 1 and not across all waves.
issues.quote: “Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].”

issues.description: Only example items are provided for SDO and RWA, not the full item sets used at each wave. Because shortened scales can differ substantially depending on item selection, this prevents replication and evaluation of construct coverage.
issues.quote: “Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] SDO6 scale.”

issues.description: The analysis is described as path analysis among three variables, but the discussion of item residual variances implies an item-level latent SEM. The manuscript does not clearly specify the measurement model, factor loadings, intercepts, residual covariances, or whether composites or latent variables were used.
issues.quote: “We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.” / “We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time”

issues.subcategory: listwise deletion incompatible with missing item
issues.description: The manuscript says one RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 and also says listwise deletion was used. If the item-level model included that item at Time 2, listwise deletion would remove all cases; if the item was omitted or handled differently, that is not reported. This creates serious uncertainty about the actual analysis.
issues.quote: “was not assessed at time two” / “Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.”

issues.description: The cross-lagged and other parameters were constrained to be time-invariant because of the authors’ substantive interest, not because stationarity was empirically supported. If effects vary across intervals, stationarity constraints can bias estimates and obscure theoretically important changes.
issues.quote: “We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.”

issues.description: The analysis section repeats the same statement about constraining cross-lagged associations and is unclear about which parameters were constrained. This impairs reproducibility and suggests possible errors in reporting the model.
issues.quote: “We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.” / “Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.”

issues.description: A standard cross-lagged panel model does not separate stable between-person differences from within-person change. Associations may reflect trait-like differences or omitted stable confounds rather than within-person prospective effects. A random-intercept CLPM or similar approach would be needed for the claimed interpretation about change.
issues.quote: “We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.”

issues.description: The model includes only SDO, RWA, and environmentalism. No demographic, political, socioeconomic, cohort, or time-varying covariates are included, despite plausible confounders of ideological and environmental attitudes. This limits causal and directional interpretation.
issues.quote: “The model included three variables across five measurement points”

issues.description: If the study truly uses a national probability sample, analyses should describe whether sampling weights, clustering, stratification, or design effects were used. No such information is provided, which threatens population inference and standard errors.
issues.quote: “in a national probability sample over five years”

issues.subcategory: estimator and ordinal treatment not reported
issues.description: The manuscript reports using Mplus but does not state the estimator, whether robust standard errors were used, whether Likert items were treated as continuous or ordinal, or how non-normality was handled. These choices affect SEM estimates, fit indices, and inference.
issues.quote: “The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29]).”

issues.description: The statement that p < .05 was adopted because the sample was large is illogical and problematic. Larger samples make trivial effects statistically significant; they usually require greater attention to effect sizes and practical significance, not reliance on conventional p-values.
issues.quote: “Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.”

issues.description: The reported confidence intervals and significance levels are inconsistent with N = 374. For example, r = -.08 would not be p < .001 in a sample of 374, and the very narrow confidence intervals imply a much larger sample. This suggests that the reported sample size, results, or both are wrong.
issues.quote: “Of the 374 participants included in this study” / “WILL | -.25*** [-.27, -.22] | -.08*** [-.11, -.05] | .76”

issues.subcategory: model fit incompatible with reported N
issues.description: The reported chi-square, df, and RMSEA are not coherent with the stated sample size. With N = 374 and χ2 = 36511.73, RMSEA would be far larger than .03. This further indicates that the analysis output may come from a different dataset or is misreported.
issues.quote: “χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07)”

issues.description: The model shows very poor absolute chi-square and CFI = .86, yet is accepted by emphasizing RMSEA and SRMR. CFI below common thresholds indicates substantial misfit, and high degrees of freedom can make RMSEA deceptively favorable. Accepting the model without modification or sensitivity analysis weakens all path interpretations.
issues.quote: “Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.”

issues.description: The RMSEA point estimate is reported as .03, but the 90% CI is [.025, .026], which does not contain .03 unless the point estimate is rounded very imprecisely. This suggests reporting or transcription error.

The data analysis section says standardized parameters are presented, but the figure caption and results report unstandardized B coefficients. Standardized and unstandardized coefficients have different interpretations and cannot be mixed when comparing effects.
issues.quote: “We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.” / “Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).”

issues.description: The results report coefficient uncertainty as ‘SD’, which is inappropriate for regression/path coefficients unless these are posterior standard deviations from a Bayesian model, which is not stated. They appear to be standard errors. Mislabeling uncertainty statistics impairs interpretation.
issues.quote: “SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).”

issues.description: The formal comparison of SDO and RWA paths was non-significant, but the authors still interpret SDO as stronger based on coefficient pattern. This is statistically invalid; a non-significant equality test does not support a claim that one predictor is stronger.
issues.quote: “We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.”

issues.subcategory: incorrect claim that Wald test is not possible
issues.description: The manuscript claims a traditional Wald test is not possible because of model constraints, but equality constraints among parameters can generally be tested directly in SEM software such as Mplus. The rationale for using the alternative fit comparison is unclear and likely incorrect.
issues.quote: “Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible.”

issues.description: The authors compare lagged effects in opposite directions using unstandardized coefficients with different outcomes. Such coefficients are not directly comparable unless variables are standardized or otherwise scaled equivalently and formally tested. The text is also internally inconsistent about which direction is stronger.
issues.quote: “the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse (2(1) = 39.97, p < .001)” / “These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships, and suggest that SDO has a stonger influence on environmental attitudes over time than the reverse.”

issues.subcategory: chi-square notation and implausible test statistic
issues.description: Several chi-square difference tests are reported as ‘2(1)’ rather than χ²(1). One test statistic is extraordinarily large for the reported coefficient difference and sample size, raising concerns about transcription errors or incorrect model comparison.
issues.quote: “These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)”

issues.description: Only Time 1 means, SDs, reliabilities, and correlations are reported. A five-wave longitudinal study should report descriptives, reliabilities, missingness, and correlations at all waves so readers can evaluate stability, change, and measurement quality.
issues.quote: “Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.”

issues.subcategory: dependent correlations compared by CI non-overlap
issues.description: The manuscript infers that the SDO-environmentalism correlation is stronger than the RWA-environmentalism correlation because confidence intervals do not overlap. These are dependent correlations sharing a variable and should be compared with an appropriate test such as Williams/Steiger test or SEM constraints.
issues.quote: “the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.”

issues.description: The text states that variables were stable over time but does not provide the autoregressive coefficients in the results table or text. Reliance on an unspecified figure limits evaluation of the stability assumptions and magnitude of change.
issues.quote: “As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time”

issues.description: The table note says confidence intervals are based on 1000 iterations, but the manuscript does not describe the bootstrap or resampling procedure, whether it accounts for missingness or complex sampling, or why 1000 iterations were chosen.
issues.quote: “Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations.”

issues.description: The discussion repeatedly makes causal claims, but the study is observational and uses a conventional CLPM without experimental manipulation or adequate control of confounding. Temporal precedence alone does not establish causality.
issues.quote: “These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.”

issues.description: The conclusion states that desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism. This exceeds what can be inferred from the design and analysis, especially given model-fit problems, sample inconsistencies, and potential confounding.
issues.quote: “This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future”

issues.description: The discussion says SDO is significantly stronger than RWA, but the reported equality comparison was non-significant at p = .126. The discussion therefore overstates the evidence.
issues.quote: “In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA.”

issues.description: The strengths section claims the sample is nationally representative and highly generalizable, contradicting the methods section’s student participant-pool sample. This seriously misleads readers about external validity.
issues.quote: “Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.”

issues.description: The authors infer that environmental attitudes are driven by a ‘motivation to exploit’ or ‘desire for dominance.’ The study measures ideological attitudes and environmental concern/skepticism, not actual motives, exploitation behavior, or mechanisms linking SDO to environmental attitudes.
issues.quote: “The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority.”

issues.description: The discussion elaborates a mechanism involving environmental inequality and willingness to burden low-status groups, but the study does not measure perceived beneficiaries, environmental justice attitudes, hierarchy-enhancing motives, or allocation of hazards. The mechanism is speculative.
issues.quote: “They believe they deserve to disproportionately benefit from environmental exploitation and avoid environmental hazards, while disregarding the effect this has on lower-status social groups.”

issues.description: The manuscript interprets RWA effects as reflecting submission to authority and tradition, but RWA also includes aggression/conventionalism and the six-item scale is not decomposed into dimensions. The stated mechanism is not directly tested.
issues.quote: “influenced to a lesser extent by the desire to submit to authority and tradition.”

issues.description: A cross-lagged association from RWA to SDO is interpreted as evidence that New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance. The analysis does not measure socialization processes, national ideology exposure, or causal mechanisms, and the sample may not represent New Zealanders.
issues.quote: “Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.”

issues.subcategory: alternative explanations acknowledged but not integrated
issues.description: The discussion acknowledges that third variables could explain the bidirectional associations, but the main conclusions still use causal language. This inconsistency weakens the interpretation and should temper claims throughout.
issues.quote: “Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable.”

issues.description: Some statistically significant paths are very small, particularly the RWA-to-environmentalism path. The manuscript emphasizes significance and causal meaning without discussing whether effects are substantively meaningful.

issues.subcategory: analysis code not available at review
issues.description: The Mplus syntax is promised only upon acceptance. For a complex model with serious ambiguities, reviewers and readers need the syntax to evaluate model specification, constraints, missing-data handling, and reproducibility.
issues.quote: “A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.”

issues.description: If the sample consists of first-year psychology students averaging 19 years old, five-year changes may reflect developmental transitions in emerging adulthood. The model does not account for age, cohort, education, or life-stage changes that could affect both ideology and environmental attitudes.
issues.quote: “the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31)”

issues.description: The methods state p < .05 as the significance threshold, but the figure caption states paths meet p < .01 unless otherwise noted. Inconsistent thresholds create ambiguity about which effects are considered statistically significant.
issues.quote: “we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05” / “All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.”
